hops.afterHeading: Two processes decide when you sleep
hops.title: Why going to bed early can be surprisingly hard
hops.text: Try turning in two hours early before a dawn flight and you may well lie there wide awake. In 1986 the sleep researcher Peretz Lavie kept volunteers up all night, then cycled them around the clock: 13 minutes awake, then 7 minutes in bed trying to sleep. Exhausted, they had the hardest time falling asleep between roughly 8 and 10 PM, a window Lavie called the "forbidden zone" for sleep. Later, sleep came on abruptly, all at once, at what he called the "sleep gate." In the lesson's model, the clock holds the upper level high in the evening, so climbing pressure has a hard time reaching it.

sources.citation: Lavie P, Electroencephalography and Clinical Neurophysiology 63(5):414-425 (1986).

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A young adult lying wide awake under a quilt in a dim dorm room at dusk, with a packed suitcase by the door.
image.caption: The clock's evening wake signal before habitual bedtime can make it hard to fall asleep early.

hops.title: How REM sleep was almost called JEM sleep
hops.text: REM sleep was nearly called JEM sleep. In late 1951 the graduate student Eugene Aserinsky attached EEG and eye-movement electrodes to his own eight-year-old son and recorded him all night. From watching sleeping infants, he expected quiet stretches with no eye movement. Instead he found stretches of vigorous, darting eye movement lasting about twenty minutes. He first meant to call them "Jerky Eye Movement," or JEM, periods, then settled on REM. His advisor, Nathaniel Kleitman, played the skeptic and demanded airtight proof. The result cut against his own theory: REM sleep came with an active cortex, and Kleitman had held that sleep was entirely passive.

sources.citation: Aserinsky E, Journal of the History of the Neurosciences 5(3):213-227 (1996).

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A vintage chart recorder on a lamp-lit laboratory desk tracing wavy ink lines on a long paper roll.
image.caption: An all-night recording in 1951 turned up stretches of rapid eye movement during sleep, later named REM.

hops.afterHeading: The switch: why sleep comes in one block
hops.title: Why the older allergy pills make people drowsy
hops.text: Histamine sounds like a runny-nose problem, but the histamine neurons of the tuberomammillary nucleus are also one of the wake-promoting groups on the awake side of the switch. In PET scans, an oral dose of diphenhydramine, the older antihistamine in Benadryl, reached the brain and occupied about 56 percent of cortical H1 histamine receptors, and the drug is well known for causing drowsiness. In a separate scan study, fexofenadine, sold as Allegra, occupied essentially none, and volunteers rated themselves no sleepier than on placebo. Both are antihistamines; in these scans they differed sharply in how much they bound to histamine receptors in the brain.
